BUSINESS 02 · BUILDING MATERIAL

Spent substrate and pumice,
bound into a fire-safe panel

We add pumice, a volcanic stone, to spent mushroom substrate and let mycelium bind it into one piece — a light, fire-resistant interior material made from what used to be waste.

Co-development inquiry→
Home/Business/Fire-safe Building Material

WHY IT MATTERS

Wasted substrate, tougher fire rules

Mushroom farms leave behind large volumes of spent substrate that cost money to dispose of, while fire-safety rules for interior materials keep getting stricter. We aim to solve both with one material: inorganic pumice raises fire resistance, and mycelium works as a natural binder.

DESIGN GOALS

What we are designing for

These are design targets; figures will be published after certified testing.

01

Fire resistance

Inorganic pumice lowers the share of combustible organic matter.

02

Lightweight

Porous pumice and mycelium aim at a light panel.

03

Circular input

Spent mushroom substrate is upcycled as the main input.

04

Non-toxic binding

Mycelium, not synthetic glue, binds the particles.

PROCESS

How it is made

  1. 01

    Collect & grind

    Spent substrate from mushroom farms is collected and ground.

  2. 02

    Mix pumice

    Pumice powder is blended into the substrate.

  3. 03

    Sterilize & inoculate

    The mix is sterilized and inoculated.

  4. 04

    Grow in molds

    Mycelium binds the mix inside molds.

  5. 05

    Dry & test

    Drying stops growth; fire and physical tests follow.

DEVELOPMENT

Development status

Inputs
Spent mushroom substrate (upcycled) + pumice
Applications
Wall and ceiling interiors; acoustic panels (to be evaluated)
Stage
Lab composition trials (4th trial in 2026)
Target tests
Non-combustible: KS F ISO 1182 · Quasi-non-combustible: KS F ISO 5660-1 · Gas toxicity: KS F 2271

This product is under development; fire classification will be confirmed by an accredited testing body.
